hints: Count the products in Fig. 5.1. One molecule of B plus two molecules of C join together with loss of two water molecules to make A, so work backwards from hydrolysis.
Remember that an ester link is $\text{COO}$ with the carbonyl from the acid and the oxygen from the alcohol, so join each $\text{COOH}$ of B to a $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}$ group from C.
walkthrough:
Spot the reverse of ester formation**
You have $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{COOH}$ plus $2\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ made from A plus $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. That is the classic pattern for hydrolysis of a diester. To rebuild A, remove the added water, meaning join the acid and alcohol parts back together.

Build the diester**
Take the dicarboxylic acid backbone $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{COOH}$ and replace each acidic $\text{OH}$ with $\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ from ethanol. You get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OOCCH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Draw both $\text{C=O}$ groups with a single $\text{O}$ linking to each ethyl group. That gives two ester links and the complete structure of A.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OCOCH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ with two ester $\text{COO}$ links shown correctly.

hints: Focus on what happens to the ester links in A when heated with dilute aqueous acid and water.
walkthrough:
Link reagents to reaction type**
Heating an ester with aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ splits the ester links by adding water across each $\text{COO}$ group to reform carboxylic acid and alcohol. Splitting by water is hydrolysis, and because dilute acid catalyses it, call it acid hydrolysis.

hints: Recall the products when any carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate, and note that B has two $\text{COOH}$ groups to neutralise.
walkthrough:
Apply the acid plus carbonate pattern**
Carboxylic acid plus carbonate always gives salt plus carbon dioxide plus water. Here B is diprotic, so one mole of $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{COOH}$ needs one mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to neutralise both $\text{COOH}$ groups. That gives the disodium salt $\text{NaOOCCH}_2\text{COONa}$ plus $\text{CO}_2$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, which explains the effervescence.

hints: Compare the functional groups in B and C, and recall which type of organic compound is acidic enough to release $\text{CO}_2$ from $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.
walkthrough:
Compare acid strength**
B is a carboxylic acid, strong enough to donate $\text{H}^+$ to carbonate and release $\text{CO}_2$. C is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, an alcohol. Alcohols are neutral and far weaker acids than carboxylic acids, so C cannot protonate carbonate and no effervescence is seen.
Final answer: C is not as strong an acid as B, ethanol is a neutral alcohol and too weak an acid to react with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.

hints: In step 1 $\text{Cl}$ is replaced by $\text{OH}$ to make a diol, think of the aqueous alkaline reagent that causes this substitution.
In step 2 both primary $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ groups are fully oxidised to $\text{COOH}$, think of the strong oxidising agent used hot and in acid for this change.
walkthrough:
Convert dichloride to diol**
Step 1 replaces two $\text{C-Cl}$ bonds with two $\text{C-OH}$ bonds. That is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{OH}^-$. Use aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ with heat. Aqueous is essential because you want substitution to alcohol, not elimination.

Oxidise diol to diacid**
Step 2 changes $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{COOH}$. Each primary alcohol needs full oxidation to a carboxylic acid. Use acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heated under reflux so no volatile aldehyde escapes before full oxidation.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, heat
step 2: acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, heat under reflux

hints: Look at how the oxygen content increases and hydrogen content changes when $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ becomes $\text{COOH}$.
walkthrough:
Recognise gain of oxygen**
Going from an alcohol to a carboxylic acid adds oxygen and removes hydrogen from carbon. Gain of oxygen is oxidation, so step 2 is an oxidation.

hints: Recall which powerful hydride reagent is needed to reduce a carboxylic acid all the way to a primary alcohol, since $\text{NaBH}_4$ is not strong enough.
walkthrough:
Pick the strong reducer**
Carboxylic acids are very resistant to reduction. $\text{NaBH}_4$ will not touch them. You need lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_4$, in dry ether, which supplies hydride to reduce $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

hints: Each $\text{COOH}$ reduced to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ needs four $[\text{H}]$, so think what the carbon skeleton product D will be from $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{COOH}$.
Balance oxygen by adding water on the right, then balance hydrogen atoms to find the total $[\text{H}]$ needed for two $\text{COOH}$ groups.
walkthrough:
Draw product D**
Reduce both $\text{COOH}$ groups to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ while keeping the central $\text{CH}_2$ unchanged. You get $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, propane-1,3-diol.

Balance with [H]**
Write $$\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{COOH} + 8[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms: 4 O on each side, and 4 H from acid plus 8[H] equals 12 H, matching 8 H in diol plus 4 H in $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Each $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ uses $4[\text{H}]$, so two groups need $8[\text{H}]$.

hints: Recall what $\text{PCl}_5$ does to an $\text{OH}$ group, and apply it to both $\text{OH}$ groups in D.
walkthrough:
Replace OH by Cl**
$\text{PCl}_5$ converts each alcohol $\text{OH}$ into $\text{Cl}$, giving misty fumes of $\text{HCl}$. D is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, so both ends become $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. The product E is $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, named 1,3-dichloropropane.
